newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin seeks end to rivalries, health fears ease.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin seeks end to rivalries, health fears ease.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday ordered a halt to bickering which has split the Kremlin while he awaits a heart operation, and a spokesman dismissed reports that his condition had deteriorated.

"Preparations for the operation are going according to plan," spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news conference in the Kremlin, denying rumours that Yeltsin had a blood problem which might delay surgery.

The 65-year-old president moved relatively freely in brief television footage showing him giving President Saparmurat Niyazov of Turkmenistan a bear-hug on Tuesday at the Barvikha sanatorium where he is staying outside Moscow.

Yeltsin also had his regular weekly meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chermomyrdin at Barvikha and was shown chatting and smiling with the premier. But his words were barely audible in the broadcast.
The president has hardly set foot in the Kremlin since his reelection on July 3, and his absence has prompted a power struggle which the president has usually sought to play down.

In a rare open sign of Yeltsin's alarm at the infighting, Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was worried by a dispute between Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov and Security Council secretary Alexander Lebed over a peace deal in breakaway Chechnya.
In other squabbles, former officials from Yeltsin's administration have traded corruption charges which some Russian politicians say are part of the complex power struggle.

"The president knows about all these verbal duels, accusations and counter-charges...The president is concerned by elements of confrontation on the public political stage, moreover confrontation between members of the same team," he said.

"In connection with this Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) ordered the prime minister, the Security Council secretary and the interior minister to agree their position before closed hearings start in the State Duma on the Chechen problems."
The hearings in the Duma, the opposition-dominated lower house of parliament, went ahead as planned but details were not immediately available.

Kulikov says the peace agreement which Lebed signed on August 31 to end nearly 21 months of fighting in breakaway Chechnya amounted to Moscow's capitulation. Lebed blames the interior minister for failing to halt fighting sooner.
Lebed was heckled and jeered in parliament this month when he defended the deal, which sets out terms for a Russian troop withdrawal which his critics describe as humiliating.
The open squabbles have heightened talk of bitter rivalries in the Kremlin as officials jockey for position in case Yeltsin proves too sick to govern and an early election is called.
Yastrzhembsky, laughing and joking with reporters, dismissed the latest rumour about the president's condition, on which some Russian shares fell.
He denied a report by Ekho Moskvy radio that Yeltsin's haemoglobin levels were so low that few surgeons would recommend an operation in the foreseeable future.
Haemoglobin is the colouring that produces the red colour of blood and plays a key role in carrying oxygen around the body.

"Nobody anywhere has talked about a change in plans for the period either before or after the operation," Yastrzhembsky said. "In the last few weeks there has been a considerable improvement in the qualitative indicators of the composition of the president's blood."
